doc.title: Denny Zeitlin interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Francisco, California, August 8, 2002

title: Encouragement from Billy Taylor, George Russell and Bill Evans
summary: He recounts three pivotal meetings: Billy Taylor at his home, studying the Lydian concept with Russell, and Bill Evans critiquing his first trio album.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: on the near west side. And again, because I was tall I could get in there, and I remember just spending nights listening to the Billy Taylor Trio and it just was wonderful music. Then I got a chance to hear Oscar Peterson at the London House in Chicago, which used to be a wonderful supper club. And I remember not only being knocked out by Oscar but even more so by Ray Brown, just the force and the drive of that playing, and I was thinking gee I hope someday I can play with a bass player like that. So I would say that those were my earliest pianistic influences along with Bud Powell. Because I heard Bud a little bit after I’d been listening to Billy Taylor and Bud knocked me out too. But then I very quickly was listening even more to Miles and to Coltrane and to Charlie Parker and I loved drummers and bass players and I’d played some bass, played some drums, played some high school and college type gigs on both instruments because I wanted to get an idea of what all the instruments were that play in a trio. And I enjoyed that very much. And then a big influence was George Russell as a composer and as a theorist. In fact when I think back over my career in terms of pivotal moments with certain musicians that were most encouraging to me and most galvanizing for me, I think of my relationship with Billy Taylor when I was just 15 or 16 years old, his graciousness. At one point my folks had his whole trio over to our home for dinner when they were in town. And I played some music with my fledgling trio for Billy. And they played for us. And it was just so warm and so encouraging, and I do remember his honestly saying that the life of an itinerant jazz musician was extremely arduous and that he had a telephone relationship with his wife back then. That was very painful. And he seemed to be saying be a doctor and enjoy your music. And through the years Billy has been an inspiration and a big support. When he first started doing some of his work as a DJ he would play my albums and stuff and then it was a big thrill a few years back to do a “CBS Sunday Morning” with him. So he’s a wonderful man. Then I think of my relationship with George Russell when I was in medical school on this fellowship in 1963 where I got together with him and studied his Lydian concept. But even more than studying the specifics of his theory, the opportunity to hang out with George and to feel his excitement about music and his excitement about what I was trying to do, the support of that, was tremendous. And then there was a time after I finished my first trio album for Columbia, which was in 1963. This was an album called “Cathexis.” I had read a review, a blindfold test that Bill Evans had done. And one of the tunes played for him was a tune from my very first album for Columbia where I was a featured pianist with Jeremy Steig. It was an album called “Flute Fever.” And Bill had really liked my playing on that. So I felt enboldened to call him up when I was in New York and say, “Bill I’ve just finished this trio album, I’ve always admired your music tremendously, I would love to meet you and have you hear this, and I would just love to get a critique, just whatever you would have to say about it.” And he

invited me over and listened to the album, and was just beautiful about it. I mean Bill was always so comfortable with his own playing, I mean even though he was very self- critical, but he knew his playing. So he didn’t have to be competitive with anybody, he didn’t have to get into putting people down or anything. So he just encouraged me to do my thing. He said, “look I don’t have anything to suggest except play your music. You’re doing it. Just keep doing your music.” And that was a tremendous encouragement from somebody, again, I had admired so much. So when I think back, the meetings with those three people at different points in my career early on was very, very inspiring.
